addressed_problems.content: The study examined quantization (PTDQ, PTSQ, QAT) and pruning (L1 and L2 with DepGraph) on five DRL algorithms (TRPO, PPO, DDPG, TD3, SAC) exclusively in continuous-action Mujoco environments (HalfCheetah, HumanoidStandup, Ant, Humanoid, Hopper). It remains unresolved whether the observed compression effects—including the superiority of PTDQ, the preference for L2 pruning, and the limited energy/memory savings—generalize to discrete-action domains such as video-game RL tasks, where task-specific methods like action quantization or different architecture choices may be required.

The experiments were conducted in six simulated Mujoco environments, leaving untested whether the model-size reductions achieved by pruning and quantization translate into measurable improvements in battery life, inference latency, and operational safety when deployed on physical hardware such as robots or drones in real-world tasks, where environmental stochasticity and hardware constraints introduce additional challenges.

The study identified that the software and runtime maturity of compression toolchains limits practical resource gains: for example, PyTorch pruning only masks parameters rather than performing true structural removal, and quantization runtimes (e.g., ONNX) introduce overhead that can increase memory usage and energy consumption. It remains an open question whether improved library-level support for genuine integer execution, efficient structural removal, and optimized runtime implementations would alter the trade-offs, potentially enabling the energy and memory benefits that were not observed in the current experiments.

The work applied post-hoc compression (quantization and pruning) to pretrained DRL models without modifying the training workflow. Whether iterative sparse training, advanced quantization-aware training schedules, or task-specific knowledge distillation could recover the performance lost during compression while simultaneously enabling practical energy savings remains unexplored and constitutes an open question.

The authors found that the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) does not hold for the DRL models studied: only 20% of models survived 50% pruning, and many models degraded after just 5% pruning. This raises the unresolved question of whether alternative pruning criteria, rewinding strategies, or algorithm-specific initializations could reveal trainable subnetworks in DRL that achieve baseline-level performance, a possibility not resolved in the present experiments.

Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents rely on deep neural networks to represent policies and value functions, and these networks incur substantial computation, memory, and energy costs that hinder deployment on resource-constrained platforms (e.g., mobile robots, extended-reality devices) and increase operational footprints in data centers. Established compression techniques from computer vision and language models—principally weight quantization (reducing floating-point precision) and pruning (removing low-importance neurons/weights)—promise smaller models and faster inference, but their effects in the peculiar setting of DRL are not well characterized. Prior work in DRL has proposed specialized discretization or compression schemes, and system implementations of quantization/pruning exist in mainstream libraries; however, those prior approaches either target discrete action/state problems, rely on task-specific distillation, or have implementation limitations (for example, some pruning libraries only mask parameters instead of physically removing them). Consequently, it remains unclear for continuous-control DRL tasks whether: (i) standard quantization modes (post-training dynamic, post-training static, quantization-aware training) preserve episodic returns; (ii) pruning with common criteria ($L_1$, $L_2$) can substantially reduce parameter count while maintaining performance; (iii) reductions in model size translate into lower inference time, memory footprint, or energy use in realistic software/hardware stacks; and (iv) hypotheses about extreme sparsification (e.g., the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis) apply in DRL. These gaps prevent practitioners from making evidence-based choices about compressing DRL agents for deployment and leave open whether off-the-shelf compression workflows yield meaningful resource savings without unacceptable loss of control performance.

nodes.content: In continuous-control DRL, reducing numeric precision of network parameters and activations is an attractive route to shrink model size and lower arithmetic costs. Prior quantization work from vision and language tasks suggests multiple practical approaches: post-training static quantization (calibration-based fixed quantization parameters), post-training dynamic quantization (compute quantization parameters at runtime per data batch), and quantization-aware training (simulate quantization during training). Before this study, it was not established which of these three practical quantization modes is preferable for episodic-return preservation in stochastic, closed-loop control tasks typical of DRL. Static calibration can fail if calibration data do not match the distribution encountered at inference; dynamic schemes mitigate distribution mismatch but may incur runtime overhead; QAT can reduce mismatch but requires modifying the training pipeline. Because DRL rollouts are stochastic and state distributions shift with policy changes, choosing the quantization mode without empirical evidence risked degrading control performance or incurring unforeseen resource costs. Resolving which practical quantization mode yields the most reliable preservation of average return across a representative set of DRL algorithms and environments is essential for practitioners who must trade off deployment complexity, runtime overhead, and policy performance.

Practitioners compress neural networks to reduce memory footprint, increase inference throughput, and lower energy usage on constrained devices. In supervised vision and language workloads, reduced numeric precision and structural sparsity often map to faster and lower-energy inference on optimized runtimes and accelerators. In DRL, however, the runtime behavior is shaped by stochastic rollouts, variable episode lengths, environment physics, and the maturity of library support for true parameter removal or integer-arithmetic execution. Before this study, it was unknown whether applying straightforward int8 quantization or norm-based pruning to policy and value networks in DRL would produce the same practical resource benefits observed in other domains, or whether software/runtime overheads and interaction with episode dynamics would negate size reductions. Without empirical measures of memory, inference time, and energy under representative DRL training/inference workloads and realistic libraries, developers cannot predict whether compression will produce the intended deployment gains.

To deploy DRL agents on memory- or compute-limited platforms, structural pruning (removing neurons/filters) is a standard strategy; common normative criteria are $L_1$ and $L_2$ magnitude-based importance scores. Prior literature provides mixed evidence about which norm yields better pruning fidelity in supervised tasks, and DRL introduces additional sensitivity because small weight changes can affect closed-loop stability and episodic return. Before this work, there was no broad empirical guidance across multiple DRL algorithms and continuous-control environments about which simple norm-based pruning criterion better preserves control performance for a given pruning budget, nor about safe default pruning magnitudes practitioners could adopt to reduce parameters without large return degradation. This lack of guidance hampers safe compression for robotics and embedded control where reliability is critical.

A practical question for compression is whether DRL networks admit very high sparsification while maintaining near-original performance, as this would permit aggressive model-size reduction for edge deployment. Previous reports in other domains suggested aggressive pruning may be possible, but DRL's closed-loop, stochastic nature could make policies fragile to large structural changes. Without systematic experiments that enforce a concrete performance-preservation constraint (here, ≥90% baseline average return) and search pruning percentages, practitioners lack empirical benchmarks indicating which DRL tasks and algorithms can safely accept large parameter reductions and which cannot.

The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis posits that within a randomly initialized dense network there exists a sparse subnetwork that, when trained in isolation with its original initialization, can match the dense network's performance. LTH has been studied primarily in supervised learning tasks; its applicability to DRL is consequential because if LTH held, one could find small trainable subnetworks for DRL and train them from scratch, dramatically reducing training and deployment cost. Prior to this study, it was unclear whether DRL networks trained for continuous control would contain such lottery tickets because DRL training dynamics, non-stationary data distributions, and sensitivity to exploratory behavior might prevent small subnetworks from achieving comparable returns. Establishing whether LTH holds in DRL is therefore critical for deciding whether extreme sparsification strategies that rely on LTH are viable for control problems.

Across the evaluated combinations of five DRL algorithms (TRPO, PPO, DDPG, TD3, SAC) and five continuous-control Mujoco environments, Post-Training Dynamic Quantization (PTDQ) produced the best average return more frequently than Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) or Post-Training Static Quantization (PTSQ), while PTSQ produced the lowest average returns most often. Measured over the reported experiment set, PTDQ achieved the best quantized outcome in 40% of the quantized models, QAT in 36%, and PTSQ in 24% of the quantized models.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that PTDQ yields the highest average return most frequently, with QAT intermediate and PTSQ worst, is primarily threatened by two compounding weak points: the confound between quantization method and library (P1) and the complete absence of statistical uncertainty quantification (P2). P1 is a show-stopper because it undermines the causal attribution of the ranking to quantization mode; even after removing P2, the comparison would not be interpretable. P2 is also high-necessity (p2=0.8) because without error bars the small margins in the count ranking could easily flip. The systematic sweep (H1) provides breadth but does not offset these threats: breadth does not resolve the library confound or statistical noise. The interaction is compounding (both threaten the same layer of comparative ranking). The dominant risk is that the true ranking, after controlling for library and uncertainty, could be very different; the highlights only confirm that the trend is observed across many points but do not protect against the specific failure modes identified. The prior probability for the conclusion is set low at 0.35 because the empirical basis is fundamentally compromised.

nodes.title: PTDQ most often yields highest average return; PTSQ performs worst; QAT intermediate

nodes.content: Converting 32-bit floating-point deep reinforcement learning (DRL) models to int8 quantized representations and applying structural pruning reduced model size, but across the tested software and hardware stack these size reductions did not reliably translate into lower energy consumption, lower memory usage, or faster inference. Quantized models frequently showed unchanged or increased memory utilization, attributed to library and runtime overhead; energy consumption only decreased in cases where the average return fell substantially, causing earlier episode termination and less computation. Pruning reduced model size but did not consistently accelerate inference or reduce measured Joules per inference.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that quantization and pruning reduce model size but not energy or memory is supported by resource measurements (Figures 1-3) but is exposed by the lack of energy measurement methodology (P3, high necessity 0.8) and the speculative attribution of energy decreases to early termination without episode-length data (P7, moderate necessity 0.6). P3 is the dominant risk: if the energy measurements are unreliable, the entire claim about energy efficiency is unsupported. P7 targets a subsidiary claim (the mechanism of energy decrease) but does not collapse the main claim that energy does not improve. There are no highlights that independently validate the resource measurements (no cross-tool verification, no sensitivity analysis). The interaction is cumulative: P3 threatens the direct empirical basis, while P7 threatens the explanatory layer. Without reliable measurements, the conclusion reduces to a claim about model-size reduction only, which is already well-established. The prior is set at 0.50 because the model-size reduction claim is solid (evident by architecture), but the energy/memory claims are empirically unvalidated.

nodes.title: Quantization and pruning reduce model size but do not reliably improve energy or memory usage

nodes.content: For the evaluated continuous-control DRL algorithms and environments, $L_2$-norm based pruning outperformed $L_1$-norm pruning in the majority of model-environment pairs: $L_2$ pruning was the selected optimal method more often, and a modest $L_2$ pruning level on the order of 10% parameter removal frequently achieved near-baseline average returns while maximizing pruning percentage within the constraint of preserving at least 90% of baseline return. Exceptions exist (notably some PPO instances and specific environments), but overall $L_2$ pruning provided a more favorable trade-off between parameter reduction and return preservation.

metadata.narrative: The preference claim for $L_2$ pruning is built on a systematic grid (H2) but is severely weakened by the lack of uncertainty quantification in Table 2 (P4, p2=0.8). P4 is high-necessity because if point estimate differences are within noise, the counting favoring $L_2$ could reverse. H2 provides a detailed comparison across 14 levels and both norms, which preempts the failure mode of evaluating only a few percentages, but does not address statistical reliability. The interaction is partially offsetting: the grid rules out coarse-granularity artifacts, but the individual cell variances are unaccounted for. The residual risk is that the preference for $L_2$ is a fragile pattern driven by noise; the conclusion is thus supported only at the qualitative pattern level, not as a reliable ranking. The prior of 0.40 reflects that the pattern is plausible and consistently observed across many points, but lacks the statistical grounding to be confident.

nodes.title: $L_2$ pruning is generally preferred; modest $L_2$ pruning (~10%) often beneficial

nodes.content: Using the selection criterion of retaining at least 90% of baseline average return while maximizing prune percentage, several model–environment combinations achieved optimal pruning percentages up to 70%, demonstrating that substantial parameter reduction is feasible without exceeding a 10% loss in episodic return for particular algorithm/environment pairs; however, this ability is heterogeneous across algorithms and environments (PPO generally had lower pruning thresholds).

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that many pairs tolerate up to 70% pruning with ≤10% return loss is directly observable from the point estimates in Table 2 and Table 3, giving it qualitative face validity. The main weak point is the arbitrary 90% threshold combined with no uncertainty propagation (P5, p2=0.7). This threatens the quantitative precision and replicability but not the qualitative direction: some pairs clearly achieve high pruning with modest return drops (e.g., TRPO Ant 70% with pruning return 979.42 vs baseline 768.97 – actually higher). P5's failure mode is refinement rather than collapse: the exact optimal percentages may shift, but the claim that "many pairs tolerate high pruning percentages" survives (though the specific value "70%" is fragile). The fine-grained grid (H2 for conclusion 3 also supports this through similar data, but H2 is not directly targeting conclusion 4; no highlight is listed for conclusion 4. The prior of 0.55 reflects that the broad qualitative pattern is supported but the numerical specifics and reproducibility are uncertain.

nodes.title: Many model–environment pairs tolerate high pruning percentages (up to 70%) while retaining ≥90% baseline return

nodes.content: The empirical pruning results contradict the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) for the evaluated DRL settings: many models suffered large performance degradation after moderate pruning, and approximately 80% of the models in the experiments did not preserve baseline-level performance after 50% pruning, indicating that small subnetworks found by magnitude pruning at substantial sparsities did not reproduce original performance when trained or evaluated in isolation under these DRL conditions.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis is not supported for these DRL experiments is invalid because the experimental protocol does not test LTH (P6, prior 0.95 for the premise being true, p1=0.95 and p2=1.0). The test uses post-training pruning, which is orthogonal to LTH's requirement of training the subnetwork from scratch with rewound initialization. This is a measurement error: the wrong quantity is measured. Consequently, the conclusion has negligible credibility regardless of any empirical numbers. No highlight redeems this because no aspect of the experiment aligns with the LTH protocol. The prior is set at 0.05 to indicate that the claim is almost certainly false as stated; a correct restatement would be "post-training magnitude pruning at moderate levels degrades performance, which does not contradict LTH."

nodes.title: Lottery Ticket Hypothesis not supported for these DRL experiments

nodes.content:
For the evaluated five DRL algorithms (TRPO, PPO, DDPG, TD3, SAC) and five continuous-control MuJoCo environments (HalfCheetah, HumanoidStandup, Ant, Humanoid, Hopper), Post-Training Dynamic Quantization (PTDQ) and Post-Training Static Quantization (PTSQ) were implemented via the ONNX Runtime library, while Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) was implemented via PyTorch; the quantized average returns therefore reflect differences not only in quantization mode but also in the inference runtime framework (ONNX vs PyTorch), and the two libraries differ substantially in operator implementations, numerical handling, and potential for optimizing quantized computation.Table 1
      ONNX Runtime (see footnote 7); PyTorch (see footnote 5)

metadata.failure_mode: If the library confound is real — e.g., ONNX Runtime's quantization pathway is better optimized for these MuJoCo networks than PyTorch's QAT pathway, or vice versa — then the counting comparison in Table 1 (PTDQ best in 40%, QAT in 36%, PTSQ in 24%) reflects library choice rather than quantization-mode superiority. The conclusion that PTDQ generally yields higher average return than QAT collapses, and the practical recommendation to prefer PTDQ over QAT for DRL would be unsupported; the observed difference could reverse if both were implemented in the same runtime. The conclusion is thus invalidated in its claim about quantization mode ranking.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper does not control for the library choice as a factor. PTDQ and PTSQ both run on ONNX Runtime; QAT runs on PyTorch. Any observed difference in average return could be driven by library-specific behavior (e.g., ONNX Runtime may have different default rounding modes, operator fusion, or memory layout) rather than by the quantization method itself. Since the library is a confound, the ranking of PTDQ vs QAT (40% vs 36% best-outcome counts) cannot be attributed to quantization modality alone. The authors do not test the same quantization method on both libraries, nor do they isolate the library effect. Therefore, the claim that PTDQ is "superior" is a claim about a PTDQ–ONNX combination versus QAT–PyTorch, not about quantization methods in general.

nodes.title: Library confound between quantization methods

nodes.content: For the five DRL algorithms and five MuJoCo environments, each quantization experiment was repeated at least 10 times with the same configuration, yet only point estimates (mean average return) for each quantization condition (Baseline, PTDQ, PTSQ, QAT) are provided, without any measure of dispersion (standard deviation, standard error, confidence interval, or interquartile range) that would allow assessing whether the differences between the quantization methods are statistically significant or could be explained by random variation across runs.Table 1

metadata.failure_mode: If the unreported standard deviations are large relative to differences between methods, many of the "best" count assignments could flip: e.g., if QAT's 36% is statistically tied with PTDQ's 40% once uncertainty is accounted for, the qualitative claim that PTDQ is broadly preferable loses its quantitative basis. The conclusion's key comparative ranking — "PTDQ superior to QAT and PTSQ" — would be unsupported, leaving only that all three methods produce outputs with overlapping variability over runs. The practical guideline to prefer PTDQ would not be justified.
metadata.weakness_reason: The reported ranking (PTDQ best in 40% of cases, QAT 36%, PTSQ 24%) uses a simple count of which method gives the highest point estimate. Without error bars, it is unknown whether these point estimates are reliably separable. For example, in many pairs the differences between PTDQ and QAT are small (e.g., TRPO Ant: PTDQ 799.46 vs QAT 970.59 – actually QAT higher; TRPO HalfCheetah: PTDQ 1004.65 vs QAT 287.94 – high variance). The paper does not perform any hypothesis test or effect-size analysis. The 10+ repetitions provide data for error bars, but these are not reported. Thus, the ranking is fragile and may not replicate.

nodes.title: Lack of uncertainty quantification on average returns

nodes.content: For the five DRL algorithms and five MuJoCo environments, energy consumption (measured in Joules) of baseline, quantized, and pruned models was measured, but the paper provides no description of the energy measurement methodology — no tool (e.g., RAPL, NVIDIA-smi, external power meter), no sampling rate, no system power state, no isolation of GPU vs CPU vs DRAM power, and no monitoring of the overhead introduced by the quantization/pruning libraries themselves, making it impossible to assess whether the reported Joules-per-inference values are accurate, reproducible, or comparable across conditions.Figure 1; Figure 2; Figure 3

metadata.failure_mode: If the energy measurements are inaccurate or incomparable — e.g., measuring total system power including idle overhead that obscures compression benefits, or using a tool that misses GPU dynamic range effects — then the conclusion that "pruning and quantization do not improve energy efficiency" could be false: proper measurement might reveal savings. The second part of the conclusion — that energy only decreases when return drops — would also lack empirical support, because the measurements themselves may be too coarse to detect small differences in per-step energy. Thus the entire conclusion's energy-efficiency component could be invalid.
metadata.weakness_reason: Without a stated measurement protocol, the energy numbers are unvalidated. Different measurement tools have different accuracy (e.g., NVIDIA-smi reports GPU power with limited temporal resolution; RAPL covers CPU+DRAM but not GPU). The paper does not state which components are monitored, whether idle power was subtracted, or how the inference energy was aggregated (e.g., total energy for a fixed number of steps vs until episode termination). The claim that energy only decreases when return drops relies on this opaque measurement; without methodological clarity, the numbers could be contaminated by measurement artifacts or systematic biases across runtime libraries (ONNX vs PyTorch).

nodes.title: Energy measurement method unspecified

nodes.content: For the five DRL algorithms and five MuJoCo environments, pruning experiments with $L_1$ and $L_2$ norms across 14 pruning levels (5% to 70% in 5% steps) each repeated at least 10 times yield average return point estimates, and optimal pruning percentages are selected by maximizing prune percentage while retaining at least 90% of baseline return; however, no measure of dispersion (standard deviation, standard error, confidence interval) is reported, so it is unknown whether the observed differences between $L_1$ and $L_2$ outcomes at a given pruning level, or the selection of one norm over the other, are statistically reliable or driven by run-to-run variance.Table 2; Table 3

metadata.failure_mode: If the point estimates in Table 2 have substantial standard errors (e.g., ±5% of baseline), then many of the optimal pruning percentages in Table 3 could be over- or under-estimated, and the counting favoring $L_2$ could change. For example, if for TRPO Hopper the $L_2$ 45% optimal is actually 87% of baseline within error, then $L_1$ 15% might be the correct selection, changing the pattern. The conclusion that $L_2$ is generally preferred would lose its empirical basis; the recommendation of "10% $L_2$ pruning as beneficial" might also be unfounded if the uncertainty at 10% is comparable to at other levels.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's recommendation to prefer $L_2$ pruning over $L_1$ is based on counting which norm yields the optimal outcome (Table 3) and on qualitative statements ("most environments... $L_2$ pruning is preferred"). Without error bars, a tie in performance between $L_1$ and $L_2$ at the chosen threshold is possible. The selection rule (maximize prune percentage while ≥90% baseline return) depends on point estimates; if the true (population) return for $L_2$ at 55% pruning is actually 89% of baseline due to variance, the optimal would shift. The lack of uncertainty means the preference claim is not statistically grounded and could be reversed with more precise measurements or repetitions.

nodes.title: Lack of uncertainty on pruning average returns

nodes.content: For the five DRL algorithms and five MuJoCo environments, the study defines a pruning regime as "tolerating high pruning percentages" if the pruned model achieves at least 90% of the baseline model's average return (point estimate) while maximizing the pruning percentage; baseline returns are reported without error bars, and pruned returns at each of the 14 discrete pruning levels are also point estimates without dispersion, so the selection of the optimal pruning percentage is a deterministic function of noisy point estimates and a single threshold, and it is unknown whether the reported optimal percentages (e.g., 70% for TRPO Ant) would replicate if baseline or pruned returns varied within their unreported confidence intervals.Table 2; Table 3

metadata.failure_mode: If the unreported variability of baseline returns is such that the effective threshold for some pairs is actually tighter (e.g., 93% of the true baseline), then the optimal pruning percentages would be lower, and the claim of "up to 70%" might apply to only a few pairs or none. Alternatively, if discrete steps skip over a region where return degrades sharply between 65% and 70%, the permissibility of 70% pruning might be an artifact of the grid. The conclusion's practical implication — that one can safely prune up to 70% for certain algorithm–environment pairs — would be overstated or wrong, potentially leading practitioners to over-prune and exceed the 10% return loss.
metadata.weakness_reason: The threshold of 90% of baseline return is an arbitrary cutoff; different thresholds (e.g., 95% or 80%) would produce different optimal percentages. More critically, since baseline returns themselves are point estimates without uncertainty, a baseline return that is actually 5% lower than reported (within run variance) would relax the 90% condition and allow higher pruning percentages, making the conclusion more optimistic; conversely, a baseline 5% higher would tighten it. The paper does not conduct a sensitivity analysis over the threshold or propagate uncertainty. The discrete pruning levels (5% steps) also mean the true optimal might be between steps. Thus the claim that "many pairs tolerate up to 70%" is a fragile empirical statement contingent on untested assumptions.

nodes.title: Arbitrary 90% threshold without uncertainty accounting

nodes.content: For the five DRL algorithms and five MuJoCo environments, the pruning experiments apply magnitude-based pruning (either $L_1$ or $L_2$ norm) to the fully-trained baseline model and evaluate the pruned network without retraining or rewinding weights to their initialization; the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (Frankle & Carbin, 2018) specifically requires identifying a subnetwork at initialization and training it from scratch with the original initialization (weight rewinding) to achieve matching performance, whereas post-training pruning and evaluation at convergence does not constitute a test of LTH because the subnetwork is not trained in isolation with its randomly-initialized weights.Frankle & Carbin, 2018 (Reference [53])

metadata.failure_mode: If the LTH training protocol (rewinding to initialization and retraining) is not applied, the experimental findings are irrelevant to the hypothesis. The conclusion "LTH is not supported for these DRL experiments" is false as a scientific statement because the experiments do not address LTH; the correct conclusion would be "post-training pruning at moderate levels degrades performance, which is consistent with many supervised learning findings but does not test LTH." The paper's claim that LTH is contradicted is entirely unsupported, and the practical implication (that one should not expect trainable sparse subnetworks in DRL) is not grounded in evidence.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper states: "The Lottery ticket hypothesis does not hold for DRL models" based on observing performance drops after pruning and noting that 80% of models do not survive 50% pruning. However, the LTH is about trainability of subnetworks from scratch (with same initialization). Post-training pruning evaluates the pruned network's performance without retraining, which is a completely different operation — it tests whether the subnetwork, as a smaller model at convergence, performs comparably. This is not a test of whether that subnetwork could be trained from initialization to match the full network's performance. The authors conflate post-training pruning fidelity with LTH. The experiment does not match the hypothesis statement; thus the conclusion is logically invalid regardless of the empirical outcomes.

nodes.title: Experiment tests post-training pruning, not LTH rewinding protocol

nodes.content: For the five DRL algorithms and five MuJoCo environments, the study reports that energy consumption decreased for quantized and pruned models only when there was a "significant drop in average return, prompting the agent to terminate early and requiring less computation", but the paper does not provide episode-length measurements, per-step energy comparisons, or controlled experiments that isolate the effect of compression on per-inference energy from the effect of shorter episodes; the energy measurement protocol and episode lengths are not reported, so the claim that early termination drives the observed energy decrease is a post-hoc explanation rather than a demonstrated causal link.Figure 1; Figure 2; Figure 3

metadata.failure_mode: If the energy decrease is actually due to per-step energy savings (e.g., quantized operations are intrinsically more efficient) and early termination is not the main driver, the conclusion that compression does not improve energy efficiency (except through performance degradation) would be misleading: there might be genuine per-step savings that are overshadowed by episode-length changes. Conversely, if early termination is indeed the mechanism, the practical implication is that energy savings from compression in DRL come at the cost of performance degradation, which is a different and more nuanced statement than "compression does not improve energy efficiency". The conclusion as stated is at risk of misrepresenting the trade-off.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper states the relationship in the Discussion: "Energy consumption tends to decrease only when there is a significant drop in average return, prompting the agent to terminate early and requiring less computation." This asserts a causal mechanism: compression reduces return -> earlier termination -> fewer timesteps -> less energy. However, no data on episode lengths is presented, and no comparison of per-step energy is made. It could be that compression reduces per-step energy but the agent explores more due to poorer performance, leading to longer episodes that offset the savings. Or the energy measurement simply records total episode energy without normalization. Without episode-length data or per-step energy analysis, the causal claim is speculative.

nodes.title: Energy decrease attributed to early termination not directly measured

nodes.content: For each of five DRL algorithms (TRPO, PPO, DDPG, TD3, SAC) and each of five continuous-control MuJoCo environments (HalfCheetah, HumanoidStandup, Ant, Humanoid, Hopper), three quantization modes (PTDQ, PTSQ, QAT) are compared, yielding 25 algorithm–environment–method combinations for which average returns are reported in Table 1; the combinatorial coverage across multiple algorithm families (on-policy, off-policy) and environment dynamics provides a broad characterization of quantization performance trends that is more extensive than previous studies in DRL compression.

metadata.credit: This systematic sweep preempts the failure mode of overgeneralizing from a single algorithm or environment; had only one or two pairs been tested, the conclusion about PTDQ superiority could be dismissed as narrow. The breadth (25 pairs) provides a basis for ranking trends, even though the ranking itself is weakened by statistical uncertainty (P2) and the library confound (P1). Without this sweep, the conclusion would lack empirical breadth; with it, at least the direction (PTDQ tends to be among the top two) is more credible across a variety of settings. The layer underwritten is generalization / extrapolation scope: the claim about PTDQ's relative standing is not a narrow artifact of one algorithm–environment pair.

nodes.title: Systematic evaluation across 5 algorithms x 5 environments

nodes.content: For each of five DRL algorithms and five MuJoCo environments, pruning is evaluated with both $L_1$-norm and $L_2$-norm importance scores across 14 discrete pruning percentages (5%, 10%, 15%, …, 70%) with the 90%-of-baseline-return selection criterion, providing a dense comparison that captures the trade-off curve between parameter reduction and return preservation under both norms, which goes beyond typical pruning studies in DRL that test only one norm or a small set of percentages.

metadata.credit: This fine-grained grid, combined with the breadth of 25 algorithm–environment pairs, supports the observation that $L_2$ pruning is preferred across most pairs and that a modest 10% $L_2$ pruning often yields near-baseline returns. The grid covers the region where optimal percentages are likely to lie (5%-70%), reducing the risk of missing the optimal due to coarse steps. Without this grid, the claim about $L_2$ preference would rest on a few arbitrarily chosen percentages; the grid allows a more robust comparison. However, the lack of uncertainty quantification (P4) still limits the credit: the grid shows the pattern at the level of point estimates, but statistical reliability remains unresolved.

nodes.title: Fine-grained pruning grid with both L1 and L2 norms across 14 percentages

steps.reasoning: Define terms used in the quantization comparison: "Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)" denotes learning policies for sequential decision problems using deep neural networks; "Post-Training Dynamic Quantization (PTDQ)" denotes a post-training quantization procedure in which quantization parameters (scale $S$ and zero point $Z$) for activations are computed at runtime per data batch; "Post-Training Static Quantization (PTSQ)" denotes a post-training, calibration-based quantization procedure that computes fixed quantization parameters $S$ and $Z$ from a calibration dataset and reuses those parameters at inference; and "Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)" denotes a training-time procedure that simulates quantization during training by rounding intermediate values to integer representations while maintaining floating-point computations to adapt weights to quantization effects.

Specify the experimental scope that produced the data supporting the conclusion: five DRL algorithms were evaluated—TRPO, PPO, DDPG, TD3, and SAC—and five continuous-control Mujoco environments were used—HalfCheetah, HumanoidStandup, Ant, Humanoid, and Hopper—and each experiment was repeated at least 10 times under the same configuration to obtain average-return estimates.

Describe how quantization was applied and evaluated: linear quantization was applied to convert $32$-bit floating-point weights/biases/activations into int8 representations using the three practical modes (PTDQ, PTSQ, QAT); for PTDQ and PTSQ the implementation computed scale $S$ and zero point $Z$ for activations only, with PTSQ using calibration to fix $S$ and $Z$ ahead of inference and PTDQ recomputing them dynamically at runtime; QAT pseudo-quantized networks during training and then exported final models to an integer-representation runtime for evaluation.

Explain the evaluation metric and data source used to compare the three quantization modes: the primary performance metric was average episodic return (average return), and the per-algorithm/per-environment average returns for baseline, PTDQ, PTSQ, and QAT are reported in the authors' tabulated results; the quantitative returns for each algorithm and environment are presented in the table labeled "Table 1", which lists baseline and the three quantized-mode average returns for every model–environment pair.
Table 1

Extract the empirical pattern visible in the tabulated returns: for many of the model–environment rows in Table 1 the PTDQ column contains the numerically best (largest) average-return value among the three quantized modes more often than QAT or PTSQ; conversely, PTSQ frequently produces the lowest average-return value among the three quantized modes in numerous rows; QAT attains the best quantized outcome in a sizable fraction of rows but not as often as PTDQ in the aggregated counts reported.
Table 1

Report the aggregated counts that summarize the relative frequency with which each quantization mode produced the best quantized average return: counted over the full set of quantized models evaluated in Table 1, PTDQ achieved the best quantized outcome in $40\%$ of the quantized models, QAT in $36\%$, and PTSQ in $24\%$; these percentages are the summary statistics the authors present to support the claim that PTDQ most often yields the highest average return, PTSQ performs worst, and QAT is intermediate.
Table 1

Record the authors' explanatory hypothesis for why PTSQ underperforms and PTDQ tends to perform better: because PTSQ fixes quantization parameters $S$ and $Z$ based on calibration data, distribution mismatch between calibration data and the stochastic, shifting state distributions encountered during DRL rollouts can cause degraded return for PTSQ; PTDQ mitigates this distribution-shift sensitivity by computing activation quantization parameters dynamically at runtime, and QAT can reduce mismatch by simulating quantization during training but requires modifying the training pipeline.

Define the resource metrics and compression techniques: "memory usage" denotes the resident memory in megabytes used by the model and runtime; "inference time" denotes wall-clock time per inference measured in seconds; "energy consumption" denotes Joules expended during inference measurements; "int8 quantization" denotes converting $32$-bit floating-point parameters/activations to 8-bit integer representations; "pruning" denotes structural removal of neurons/filters to reduce parameter count.

Summarize the software/hardware stack and measurement procedure that produced the resource data: experiments were run on hardware comprising NVidia RTX 4090 GPUs (24GB VRAM), 256GB RAM, and an Intel Core i9 CPU, with quantization implemented using ONNX Runtime for PTDQ/PTSQ and PyTorch for QAT, and pruning implemented using the torch-pruning package integrated with a dependency-graph-based structural pruning approach; memory, inference time, and energy were measured for baseline and compressed models and are reported in the paper's figures and tables.

Report the observed relationship between model-size reductions and measured memory usage: although int8 quantization and structural pruning reduced the on-disk or parameter count model size, the measured memory utilization in the reported experiments did not decrease correspondingly; Figure 1 shows no decreases in memory utilization attributable to quantization in the tested platforms and, in some PTDQ and PTSQ cases, observed memory utilization increased relative to the baseline.
Figure 1

Explain the authors' attribution for unchanged or increased memory usage after quantization: the paper attributes unchanged or increased memory utilization to runtime and library overheads introduced by the quantization toolchain and by the implementation choices of quantization runtimes (for example, some runtimes add auxiliary data structures or do not perform integer-only execution), which can negate the expected memory savings from a smaller numeric representation.

Report the observed relationship between model-size reductions and measured energy consumption and inference speed: energy consumption (Joules) decreased only in cases where average episodic return fell substantially, causing episodes to terminate earlier and thus requiring fewer environment steps and less computation; otherwise, quantized or pruned models frequently showed unchanged or even increased energy consumption and did not consistently deliver faster inference.
Figure 1

Present the pruning-specific empirical outcome: structural pruning did produce model-size reductions and the authors tabulate optimal pruning percentages per model/environment in Table 3, but these pruning-induced parameter reductions did not consistently accelerate inference or reduce measured Joules-per-inference in the tested software/hardware stack; the paper reports that pruning yielded only negligible (about $1\%$) decreases in measured memory usage in aggregate.
Table 3

Make explicit the authors' practical conclusion linking the measurements to deployment implications: because standard int8 quantization and norm-based pruning reduced model size but did not reliably reduce memory utilization, inference time, or energy consumption under the selected runtimes and hardware, practitioners cannot assume that reducing parameter counts or numeric precision will produce proportional resource savings without considering runtime/library maturity and the potential for distribution-driven changes in episode length that affect compute.

Define pruning criteria and the experimental pruning workflow: "$L_1$ pruning" denotes magnitude-based importance scoring using the $L_1$ norm (sum of absolute values) to rank parameters for removal; "$L_2$ pruning" denotes using the $L_2$ norm (square-root of sum of squares or equivalently squared-norm ranking) to rank parameters for removal; structural pruning was implemented with the torch-pruning package integrated with a dependency-graph approach (DepGraph) to handle inter-layer and intra-layer dependencies so that removed structures preserve graph consistency.
[50]

State the optimization criterion used to select the "optimal" pruning method and percentage per model–environment pair: the authors selected the pruning method and pruning percentage that preserved at least $90\%$ of the baseline average return while maximizing the pruning percentage (that is, retain at least $90\%$ of baseline return and choose the largest pruning percentage that satisfies this constraint).

Describe the experimental sweep and data sources informing the comparison: pruning experiments evaluated both $L_1$ and $L_2$ criteria at pruning percentages in the set $\{5\%,10\%,15\%,20\%,25\%,30\%,35\%,40\%,45\%,50\%,55\%,60\%,65\%,70\%\}$; per-algorithm/per-environment pruned average returns and the method/percentage selected by the $90\%$-return maximization criterion are reported in the tabulated results labeled "Table 2" and summarized in "Table 3".

Extract the empirical pattern from the pruning tables and figures: across most model–environment pairs listed in Table 2 and summarized in Table 3, the $L_2$-norm based pruning selection appears more frequently as the chosen optimal method than $L_1$, indicating that $L_2$ pruning yielded more favorable trade-offs between pruning percentage and preserved average return under the authors' $90\%$ constraint.

Quantify the "modest $L_2$ pruning" recommendation: the authors observe that a modest $L_2$ pruning level on the order of $10\%$ parameter removal often achieved near-baseline average returns while allowing some parameter reduction; the paper explicitly states that "a $10\%$ reduction in DRL model size through $L_2$ pruning is beneficial" in the general case, while noting exceptions.

Acknowledge exceptions and heterogeneity: the authors note exceptions where $L_1$ pruning outperforms $L_2$ (for example, some PPO instances and specific environments) and acknowledge that the optimal criterion varies with the DRL algorithm and environment complexity; when $L_1$ outperforms $L_2$ the reported average-return values remain closely aligned.

Connect the pruning-performance observations to practical guidance: given the tabulated evidence and the $90\%$-return selection rule, the authors recommend $L_2$ pruning as a generally preferable default for the evaluated continuous-control DRL settings and recommend modest $L_2$ pruning (around $10\%$) as a practical starting point because it frequently preserves return while reducing parameters.

Define the pruning selection rule employed to identify high-pruning solutions: the authors' selection criterion is to "retain at least $90\%$ of baseline average return while maximizing prune percentage", which means for each baseline model the authors searched pruning percentages and chose the largest percentage that still produced an average return $\geq 0.9$ times the baseline average return.

Report the tabulated evidence supporting very large pruning ratios: the pruning experiments evaluated pruning percentages up to $70\%$ and Table 2 and Table 3 record many model–environment pairs whose selected optimal pruning percentage equals $70\%$ (reported as $0.7$ in the tabulation), indicating that under the $90\%$-return constraint those pairs tolerated removal of $70\%$ of parameters.

Provide concrete examples appearing in the authors' tables to illustrate the claim: for example, Table 2 shows entries with pruning percentages of $0.7$ (i.e., $70\%$) for combinations such as TRPO on Ant, DDPG on HumanoidStandup, TD3 on HumanoidStandup, and SAC on HumanoidStandup, among others; these entries are examples where substantial parameter removal still satisfied the $90\%$-return preservation constraint.

State the heterogeneity caveat: the authors explicitly note that the ability to tolerate high pruning percentages is heterogeneous across algorithms and environments—for example, PPO generally had lower pruning thresholds—so while several model–environment pairs reached pruning ratios up to $70\%$ without exceeding a $10\%$ loss in episodic return, this is not universal.

Conclude the practical implication derived from these observations: substantial parameter reduction up to $70\%$ is feasible without exceeding $10\%$ average-return degradation for particular algorithm/environment pairs in the authors' experimental set, but model-and-environment-specific evaluation is necessary due to heterogeneous tolerance.

Define the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) and the empirical test applied: the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis posits that within a randomly initialized dense network there exists a sparse subnetwork that, when trained in isolation with its original initialization, can match the performance of the dense network; the authors tested pruning at increasing sparsity levels (including $50\%$ pruning and up to $70\%$) and observed whether pruned networks preserved baseline-level average return when pruned or when small subnetworks were isolated.
[53]

Describe the experimental observations relevant to LTH: the authors observed that many models suffered large performance degradation after moderate pruning levels; specifically, the paper reports that around $40\%$ of the models fail (do not "survive") after more than $5\%$ pruning and that approximately $80\%$ of the models did not preserve baseline-level performance after $50\%$ pruning, indicating a widespread inability of pruned subnetworks to match dense-model performance in these DRL settings.
Table 2

Explain how these observations contradict LTH in the DRL experiments: because LTH predicts the existence of small subnetworks (often referenced in the LTH literature as networks of size approximately $10\%-20\%$ of the original) that can be trained in isolation to recover dense performance, the empirical finding that $80\%$ of models failed to preserve baseline performance after $50\%$ pruning, and that many models show sharp performance drops at low pruning percentages, runs counter to LTH's expectation that such trainable subnetworks commonly exist.

Record the authors' explicit conclusion and its scope: the authors conclude that their empirical pruning results contradict the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis for the evaluated DRL settings—i.e., in the studied continuous-control DRL experiments, magnitude-based pruning did not expose small trainable subnetworks that reproduce original performance when isolated or when sparsified to high sparsities.
Table 2

State any authors' caution about generalization: the authors note that this negative finding pertains to their experimental setup (selected DRL algorithms, continuous-action Mujoco environments, magnitude-based pruning, and the specific training/evaluation procedures used) and do not claim a universal refutation of LTH for all possible DRL training regimens, pruning criteria, rewinding strategies, or initialization schemes; they frame the result as empirical evidence that LTH was not supported in their experiments.

open_questions.content: The study acknowledges several unresolved issues and limitations that define directions for future work. First, the experiments were restricted to continuous-action Mujoco simulated environments; it remains unresolved whether the reported quantization and pruning behaviors generalize to discrete-action domains (e.g., many video-game RL tasks) where different compression or task-specific methods might be required. Second, the experiments used a limited set of simulated environments and did not test real-world robotic or drone platforms; whether model-size reductions translate into measurable battery-life, latency, and safety improvements on physical hardware remains open. Third, software and runtime maturity affected outcomes: many pruning and quantization toolchains (e.g., frameworks that only mask parameters rather than remove them, or quantization runtimes that add overhead) limit practical resource gains; improving library-level integer execution and true structural removal may change the measured energy and memory trade-offs. Fourth, the interaction between compression and training workflows—such as whether iterative sparse training, advanced quantization-aware schedules, or task-specific distillation could recover performance while enabling practical energy savings—was not explored and remains an open question. Finally, the negative findings regarding the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis in these settings raise the open question of whether alternative pruning criteria, rewinding strategies, or algorithm-specific initializations could reveal trainable subnetworks for DRL; this was not resolved in the present experiments.
